---
title: "Formative self-test"
description: "Eleven newly developed practice cases across all four parts of the course, each with a single best answer and an explanation that opens on demand."
---

These cases were written for practice. They are **not** questions from the course examination and do not count
towards any grade. Each case has one best answer. Decide first, write down why, then open the explanation. If your
reason differs from the explanation, the reason matters more than the letter.

All cases are fictitious; numbers are *synthetic* or *assumptions* unless a source is given.

## Part I · Clinical questions and sources

### Case 1 · Radiographs or patients?

An audit of ankle injuries in a fictitious emergency department includes 240 radiographs from 150 patients. A
fracture is visible on 60 radiographs; these belong to 45 patients.

**What proportion of patients had a fracture?**

A. 18.8% · B. 25.0% · C. 30.0% · D. 40.0% · E. It cannot be determined from these data.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**C. 30.0%** (45/150). The question is about patients, so the denominator is the 150 patients and the numerator the
45 patients with at least one fracture. A (45/240) mixes patients and radiographs; B (60/240) answers a question
about radiographs; D (60/150) counts radiographs in the numerator and patients in the denominator. E would be right
only if the radiographs could not be linked to patients.
:::

### Case 2 · A summary that says more than its source

A generated summary of the literature states: "A randomised trial showed that the triage algorithm reduced
mortality by 20%." The cited article exists and its DOI resolves correctly. It is a retrospective cohort study that
reports how well the algorithm's score discriminated between patients who died and those who survived.

**Which verdict on the evidence card is most appropriate?**

A. Supported, because the DOI resolves to the cited article.
B. Partly supported, because the article is about the same algorithm.
C. Not supported, because the study design cannot show an effect on mortality.
D. Source not found.
E. Supported, if the reported discrimination is high.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**C.** The source exists and fits the topic, but a retrospective study of discrimination says nothing about whether
using the algorithm changes mortality; that would need a comparison of patients managed with and without it,
ideally randomised. A and E confuse the existence or quality of a source with support for the specific claim. B is
too generous: the claim is about an effect the design cannot measure. D is wrong because the source was found.
:::

## Part II · Testing and comparing models

### Case 3 · The same test in a screening clinic

A test with an assumed sensitivity and specificity of 95% each is used in a screening clinic where 2% of the people
examined have the condition.

**Which value is closest to the positive predictive value?**

A. 2% · B. 28% · C. 50% · D. 72% · E. 95%

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**B. 28%.** Out of 10,000 people, 200 have the condition and 190 of them test positive; of the 9,800 without it,
5% = 490 test positive. The PPV is 190/680 = 27.9%. E confuses PPV with sensitivity, D is the share of false alerts
among all alerts, A is the prevalence. Natural frequencies make the calculation and the explanation to patients
easier.
:::

### Case 4 · Excellent inside, mediocre outside

A model classifies skin lesions from 5,000 images of 800 patients. The images were split at random into training
and test sets; test accuracy was 0.93. In a second hospital, accuracy was 0.78.

**What is the best next step to understand the gap?**

A. Train for more epochs to increase accuracy further.
B. Repeat the internal evaluation with a split by patient and report the number of test patients.
C. Report the mean of 0.93 and 0.78 as the expected accuracy.
D. Exclude the second hospital because its images look different.
E. Increase the number of test images by adding more images of the same patients.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**B.** With a random image split, images of the same patient can appear in training and test, so the 0.93 partly
measures recognition of known patients. A patient-level split shows how much of the gap is leakage and how much is
a genuine difference between hospitals. A and E make the leakage worse or hide it; C averages two different
questions; D removes exactly the evidence about transfer that is needed.
:::

### Case 5 · Good ranking, wrong level

A prediction model is applied in a new hospital. Its AUC there is 0.85. The mean predicted risk is 10%, but 20% of
patients have the outcome.

**Which statement is correct?**

A. The model is unusable because its predictions are wrong.
B. The model ranks patients well but underestimates absolute risk; thresholds based on predicted risk would miss
   patients until it is recalibrated with local data.
C. An AUC of 0.85 guarantees that the predicted risks are correct.
D. The difference is explained by chance and can be ignored.
E. The model should be retrained from scratch on the new hospital's data without any comparison.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**B.** Discrimination (ranking) and calibration (level) are different properties. A shift in calibration-in-the-large
is common when prevalence differs; updating the intercept with local data is often the first step. C confuses the
two properties; A overstates the problem; D ignores a doubling of the observed risk; E discards a model that still
ranks well and skips the comparison.
:::

## Part III · Justifying complex models

### Case 6 · A surprising protective factor

In a registry of patients admitted to a trauma intensive care unit, people with a certain chronic condition have
lower in-hospital mortality than people without it. In the general population of injured people, the condition is
not associated with lower mortality.

**What is the most likely explanation?**

A. The condition protects against death after injury.
B. Selection on intensive care admission: admission depends on both injury severity and the condition, so within
   the registry the condition is associated with less severe injuries.
C. Random error in a large registry.
D. Reverse causation: dying causes the condition.
E. Measurement error in the mortality outcome.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**B.** Intensive care admission is a collider when both severity and the chronic condition lead to admission.
Restricting the analysis to admitted patients creates an association between the condition and severity, and
therefore with mortality, that does not exist in all injured people. A draws a causal conclusion from a selected
sample; C, D and E do not explain why the pattern appears only in the registry.
:::

### Case 7 · A biomarker that seems to recover

A biomarker is measured on days 1, 7, 14 and 28 after injury in 30 patients. By day 28 only 18 patients are still
measured; the others were transferred or died, mostly the most severely injured. The mean of the measured values is
higher on day 28 than on day 1, which the authors describe as recovery.

**Which response is most appropriate?**

A. Accept the conclusion because the day-28 mean is higher.
B. Report the number of patients per day, analyse the trajectories with a mixed model and add a sensitivity
   analysis that assumes the missing patients would have had lower values.
C. Exclude all patients with missing values and analyse only the 18 complete cases.
D. Replace missing day-28 values with the day-28 mean of the other patients.
E. Report only the day-1 values, because they are complete.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**B.** The dropout is informative: the sickest patients leave the sample, so the later means describe a different,
healthier group. A mixed model uses all available measurements and is valid if dropout depends only on observed
values; a sensitivity analysis shows how far the conclusion depends on that assumption. C and D bake the bias into
the result; A ignores it; E discards the question.
:::

## Part IV · Translating models into practice

### Case 8 · Who carries the errors? (ethics)

At the proposed threshold, a fracture alert detects 81% of fractures in younger adults but 68% in people aged 75
and older, and it raises more false alerts in the older group. The intervals for sensitivity overlap.

**What is the most defensible next step?**

A. Use the threshold, because the intervals overlap and the difference may be chance.
B. Report errors for both groups with denominators, discuss the trade-off with clinicians and patient
   representatives, and plan a local evaluation that is large enough for the older group before deciding.
C. Exclude older patients from the alert.
D. Choose a separate threshold for older patients based on these numbers alone.
E. Stop the project, because any difference between groups is unacceptable.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**B.** The data suggest that one group carries more of both kinds of error, but they are too uncertain to settle
the question. Making the trade-off visible and collecting enough local evidence is the defensible step. A treats
uncertainty as reassurance; C withholds a possible benefit from the group most at risk; D over-fits a threshold to
small numbers; E ignores that usual care also distributes errors.
:::

### Case 9 · Same software, new purpose (regulation)

A hospital's research dashboard shows aggregated statistics about an alert model. It is now proposed that the
dashboard show an alert for each patient in the emergency department, prompting a second review of the image.

**Which statement is correct?**

A. Because the code is unchanged, the regulatory situation is unchanged.
B. Research software can never be a medical device.
C. Whether the software is a medical device depends on its intended purpose; the new purpose supports individual
   diagnostic decisions and must be assessed under the MDR, where Rule 11 points to class IIa or higher.
D. Because the software uses AI, only the AI Act applies, not the MDR.
E. MDCG guidance is binding law and decides the class on its own.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**C.** The MDR defines a medical device by its intended purpose (Article 2(1) and (12)), and Rule 11 in Annex VIII
classifies software that provides information used for diagnostic decisions as class IIa unless the possible
consequences are more serious. A and B ignore the role of the intended purpose; D is wrong because the AI Act
applies alongside sectoral law, which it lists in Annex I; E is wrong because MDCG documents are guidance, not law.
:::

### Case 10 · A name in the support log (data protection)

On Monday at 09:00 a hospital (the controller) learns from its software provider (the processor) that a support
ticket contained a patient's name and a short clinical note. The hospital's assessment is that the breach is likely
to result in a risk, but not a high risk, to the person concerned.

**Which course of action matches the GDPR?**

A. Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware,
   that is, by Thursday 09:00; communication to the patient is not mandatory at this risk level; document the
   assessment.
B. Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of the ticket being created.
C. Inform the patient within 72 hours; the authority does not need to be notified.
D. No action is needed because the provider, not the hospital, made the mistake.
E. Notify only if the patient complains.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**A.** Article 33 GDPR requires notification to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible,
not later than 72 hours after the controller became aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk.
Communication to the person (Article 34) is required when a high risk is likely. Both assessments are documented.
B starts the clock at the wrong moment; C reverses the two thresholds; D ignores that the hospital remains the
controller; E has no basis in the regulation. Real cases also need the institution's own procedures.
:::

### Case 11 · The model that runs is not the model you validated (security)

After a weekend update, a dashboard shows a model version that was never approved. Alert rates have doubled.

**Which control, with its test, best addresses this threat in future?**

A. A note in the operating manual asking the provider to inform the hospital about updates.
B. The service compares the checksum of the model file with a list of approved versions at start-up and refuses to
   run otherwise; a test installs a modified file on a test system and shows that the service does not start.
C. Weekly manual review of the alert rate.
D. Encryption of the model file at rest.
E. Stronger passwords for the support accounts.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**B.** The threat is to integrity: an unapproved model runs. An automated check against approved versions prevents
it, and the test shows that the check works. A depends on goodwill and cannot be tested; C detects the problem only
after harm; D protects confidentiality, not integrity; E addresses access, not which version is running.
:::
